title: When Life Learned Before It Died
deckline: For billions of years, Earth stored most durable biological information across generations. Nervous systems added a much faster write cycle: experience could alter behavior within one lifetime.
objective: Establish the series' temporal and information-system baseline: molecular life already stores, senses, signals, and responds; hereditary storage is durable but mostly generation-paced; nervous systems add much faster within-lifetime read/write; social learning then begins moving acquired information between bodies.
learning_outcomes: Keep two clocks in view: geological time for the evolution of information substrates, and information lifetime for how long a usable pattern can persist.
See hereditary molecules as durable biological storage whose ordinary update cycle is mainly generational, while molecular sensing and signaling already operate on much faster local timescales.
Understand nervous systems as a new layer that increases read/write speed, integration, and behavioral flexibility without replacing molecular signaling.
Recognize learning as a within-lifetime write operation and social learning as the next pressure: copying an update into another body.
continuity: This opening episode spans roughly three billion years of planetary history, from evidence of microbial life at least 3.5 billion years ago to animal nervous systems diversifying more than half a billion years ago, then zooms from geological time to the much faster clock of learning within one lifetime.
future_pressure: A nervous system can write experience quickly, but a private memory still dies with its carrier unless some of that update reaches another individual.

slides.title: The archive begins inside life

image.alt: A stylized young Earth above a dark ocean, descending into glowing microbial life and molecular patterns whose shapes, concentrations, and sequences carry information.

paragraphs: Start the clock at planetary scale. Earth is about 4.54 billion years old. Evidence of microbial communities reaches back at least 3.5 billion years. So this first episode is not describing centuries or even millions of years. It spans billions.

Somewhere in that deep interval, living chemistry became able to preserve reusable patterns by helping make descendants with related organization. Modern life uses DNA as its central hereditary storage, although the earliest life did not necessarily use the full modern system.

In computer language, this was astonishingly durable storage with a very slow ordinary write cycle: much of the archive changes through reproduction across generations. The metaphor is only a lens, but the contrast will matter later. Earth could now keep biological patterns long after an individual body disappeared.
That storage layer kept running for billions of years before anything resembling a nervous system appeared.

slides.title: The molecular system was already online

image.alt: A community of luminous bacteria exchanges clouds of signal molecules while one cell follows a chemical gradient and retains a fading molecular trace of earlier conditions.

paragraphs: Durable heredity was not the only clock. Cells also had fast local traffic.

Bacteria release molecules that other bacteria detect. Through quorum sensing and related systems, chemical signals can change collective behavior within and across species. An E. coli cell following a chemical gradient can also retain a fading molecular trace of recent conditions, allowing the present to be compared with moments earlier.

So the first information system already had storage, sensing, messaging, and short-lived state. Its read and write speeds depended on chemistry: molecules had to be produced, moved, detected, and translated into action.
Communication did not begin with animals. Animals inherited a planet that was already talking chemically.

slides.title: Physics sets the performance ceiling

image.alt: Molecular signals and microbial colonies fill one layer while a multicellular animal form emerges above them, showing an expanding information scale without a ladder or progress arrow.

paragraphs: Chemistry can do absurdly sophisticated things, but it cannot negotiate away physics. Molecular signals diffuse, dilute, react, and degrade. Most hereditary updates that persist widely are written on the slow clock of generations.

None of this made multicellular animals inevitable. Single-celled life remained spectacularly successful. But in some lineages, many cells began operating as one body, creating larger distances and more complicated coordination problems inside that body.

The old molecular layer stayed underneath. What changed was the performance requirement: some bodies benefited from faster long-range signaling, faster integration of sensation, and more flexible responses.
A new layer did not replace the old operating system. It extended what the system could do.

slides.title: A much faster clock appears

image.alt: Several translucent marine animals show different glowing neural organizations, from diffuse nerve nets to more concentrated signaling centers.

paragraphs: By well over half a billion years ago, animal nervous systems were already diversifying into very different organizations. They did not arrive as one prototype brain, and researchers still debate parts of their deep evolutionary origin.

For our information-system story, the important change is speed. A nervous system can connect what is happening now — light, touch, movement, internal state — to coordinated action across a body on a timescale dramatically faster than generational inheritance.
The planet now had two very different clocks running together: slow durable biological storage across generations, and fast electrical-chemical traffic inside individual lives.
Then the fast layer gained another trick: it could be changed by experience.

slides.title: Experience becomes writable

image.alt: A small box jellyfish moves through a maze of mangrove roots, with a faint failed path and a brighter altered route suggesting behavior changed by experience.

paragraphs: Learning is a write operation on the fast clock: an encounter changes what the same animal does next.

A tiny Caribbean box jellyfish gives us a useful nuisance. It has no conventional centralized brain, yet laboratory experiments showed that it could learn to avoid obstacles by combining visual and mechanical cues.
The update did not wait for reproduction. It happened during one lifetime, and the usable trace could influence later behavior minutes, hours, days, or sometimes much longer depending on the system.
Evolution still builds the machinery. But now the machinery can write part of its own operating history while it is running.

slides.title: There was never one ladder of minds

image.alt: Different animal forms — a jellyfish, an octopus-like body, an insect, and a bird-like animal — surround distinct glowing neural patterns without any hierarchy or progression arrow.

paragraphs: Animal nervous systems branched into many architectures: diffuse nets, rings, cords, ganglia, brains, and combinations that fit different bodies and environments.
So more information does not mean more human-like. A jellyfish, an insect, an octopus, and a migratory bird solve different readout problems with different sensors, memories, and response times.
The important shared upgrade is not a ladder toward us. It is that individual experience can now be stored and used on the timescale of a life.
That creates a new bottleneck: private memory is still private.

slides.title: The first copy leaves the original body

image.alt: Two stylized bumblebees face the same flower-like puzzle while layered chemical, visual, and behavioral signals connect the experienced individual to the observer.

paragraphs: Once learning exists, the next question is obvious: can that fast local write be copied?

Animals watch, follow, imitate, touch, call, vibrate, and leave traces in the environment. No single moment invented social transmission. A modern bumblebee experiment makes the principle visible: naive bees that failed to solve a two-step puzzle alone could learn the complete behavior after watching trained demonstrators.

That does not date the first social learning, and living bees are not fossils. It shows the capability clearly: information acquired during one individual's lifetime can change what another individual is able to do.
The storage system has moved from one body toward a network. Episode 2 asks how long that copied update can survive.
